“We as young people of color coming from low-income communities have not all seen ourselves in this movement,” says YVA’s education and organizing coordinator, Hannah Estrada, 20. “But we’re going to be the most impacted, so it’s important that we are involved. She adds, "What we want as young people of color is for other young people of color to see us — to highlight frontline communities."
According to YVA, centering frontline youth means meeting fellow students where they are on the issues that impact them every day.

Says Estrada, “We don’t see the climate crisis as separate from colonialism or white supremacy, but a symptom of the same system. The climate crisis intersects other issues — food deserts, poverty, violence. We can’t pretend we’re not fighting these other traumas."

She continues, "You can’t expect frontline communities to pick one issue. When we’re asking people to come into the movement, we’re not asking them to change the way they are, but to bring their whole selves and skills.”

YVA’s Points of Unity reflects this approach and includes positions against white supremacy, for the Black Lives Matter movement, abolishing the police, ICE, and the prison industrial complex, supporting Indigenous sovereignty, challenging rape culture, and providing housing, health care, and meaningful work for all.
